name: Sage

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: light, well-drained loam or sandy loam
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Sage likes well-drained loam or sandy soil that does not stay soggy.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: sandy, gritty, or shallow rocky soil of low fertility
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Sandy, gritty, or poor rocky soil is fine, as long as it drains well.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: heavy or poorly drained clay that stays wet around the roots
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Heavy, wet clay is a problem because it holds water and rots the roots.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Well-drained, medium-to-dry soil of low-to-average fertility in full sun. Sage is a Mediterranean subshrub that tolerates drought and poor ground and is intolerant of wet, poorly drained soil, so drainage matters far more than richness. Loam, sandy loam, or shallow rocky soil all suit it; amend heavy clay for drainage, or grow on a raised bed or mound, rather than feeding it up.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Sage wants well-drained soil and full sun, and it is happy in poor, dry ground. Rich, damp soil actually works against it and makes the roots rot. If your soil is heavy clay, mix in coarse material so water drains fast, or plant sage on a raised bed or mound, and go easy on the compost.

ph.note_seasoned: Sage grows best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, roughly pH 6.0 to 7.0, and tolerates neutral ground up to about 8.0. It is not fussy about pH as long as the soil drains well; drainage is the real requirement, not a precise pH.
ph.note_beginner: Sage likes soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about pH 6.0 to 7.0, and copes up to around 8.0. It is not picky about this, so do not worry much about the number as long as the soil drains well.

tip_seasoned: Treat sage lean and dry: full sun, well-drained soil, sparing water, and little to no feeding. Prune it hard each spring as new growth breaks, cutting back leggy stems but never into the bare old wood, which does not resprout well. Harvest lightly the first year, then cut sprigs freely; leaves have the strongest flavor just before the plant flowers. Even well grown, sage gets woody in a few years, so plan to replace it.
tip_beginner: The trick with sage is to keep it lean and sunny and not overwater it. Trim it back each spring when new growth starts, cutting off the leggy stems but not down into the hard woody base. Go easy on harvesting the first year, then snip sprigs whenever you cook; the flavor is best just before it flowers. Sage still gets woody after a few years, so plan to replace it now and then.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Sage needs little fertility and is easy to over-feed. A modest amount of compost worked in at planting is plenty; heavy feeding pushes soft, weak growth with diluted flavor and invites disease. In poor soil a single light spring feeding is more than enough.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Sage barely needs feeding. A little compost at planting is enough. Feeding it a lot just gives you floppy growth and weaker-tasting leaves, so skip the fertilizer for the most part.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: N/A. Sage is not fed to an N-P-K target; the goal is lean soil and minimal-to-no supplemental feeding, so no fertilizer analysis applies.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: N/A. There is no fertilizer number to hit here; the aim is to feed sage as little as possible.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: At most a light inch of compost at planting, or one light spring feeding per season in poor soil.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A little compost at planting, and usually nothing after that.

companions.note_seasoned: Sage pairs naturally with other sun-loving, low-water Mediterranean herbs that share its lean, well-drained conditions, such as rosemary, thyme, and oregano; group these together and run the whole bed dry. Its early-summer flowers draw bees and other pollinators. By tradition it is grown near cabbage-family crops and carrots, where growers believe its strong aroma helps confuse pests, though this is folk practice rather than a measured effect. Keep it away from thirsty, rich-soil neighbors whose watering would keep sage too wet.
companions.note_beginner: Plant sage next to other dry, sunny herbs like rosemary, thyme, and oregano, which want the same conditions. Its flowers bring in bees. Gardeners have long grown sage near cabbage and carrots in the hope its strong smell keeps pests away, which is tradition more than proven fact. Keep sage away from plants that need lots of water, because that wet soil will rot it.

good_seasoned.name: Rosemary
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A woody Mediterranean herb that wants the same full sun, lean soil, and sharp drainage as sage, so the two share one dry, low-water bed without cultural compromise.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Rosemary and sage are both drought-tolerant Mediterranean subshrubs needing full sun and fast drainage; growing them together lets one waterwise regime suit both and avoids the overwatering that rots sage. Shared-conditions co-cultivation. traditional/medium.

good_seasoned.name: Thyme
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A low, drought-tolerant Mediterranean herb with the same lean, well-drained, full-sun needs; a natural bedmate that keeps the whole planting on a dry schedule.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Thyme shares sage's full-sun, low-water, sharp-drainage requirements, so the pairing is sound co-cultivation with no watering conflict. traditional/medium.

good_seasoned.name: Oregano
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Another sun-loving, drought-tolerant Mediterranean herb that thrives in the same poor, well-drained soil, making it an easy companion in a dry herb bed.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Oregano matches sage's Mediterranean culture (full sun, lean soil, low water), so co-cultivation is easy and avoids overwatering. traditional/medium.

good_seasoned.name: Cabbage-family crops
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Traditionally interplanted with brassicas, where growers hold that sage's strong aroma helps deter cabbage pests; a long-standing practice rather than a measured effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Old companion-planting tradition pairs aromatic sage with cabbage-family crops to confuse or deter pests such as cabbage moths. No controlled T1 trial confirms a pest effect, so flagged low. traditional/low.

good_seasoned.name: Carrots
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional pairing in which sage's aroma is thought to help mask carrots from carrot pests; folk practice, not a documented result.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Traditional aromatic-herb-with-carrot pairing believed to deter carrot fly. Not verified by a controlled source, so low confidence. traditional/low.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Rosemary
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Likes the same sunny, dry spot as sage.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Shared Mediterranean culture co-cultivation. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Rosemary is one of the easiest sage partners because it asks for exactly what sage does: full sun, poor soil, and sparing water. Plant them together and you can run the whole bed dry, which is exactly how both stay healthy and avoid the root rot that comes from too much water.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Thyme
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Another dry, sunny herb that grows well beside sage.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Shared-conditions co-cultivation. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Thyme is a low, drought-tolerant herb that wants the same lean, well-drained, sunny conditions as sage, so the two make a natural, low-maintenance pairing you can water lightly and infrequently.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Oregano
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Thrives in the same poor, well-drained soil as sage.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Shared culture co-cultivation. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Oregano is a sun-loving Mediterranean herb happy in poor, fast-draining soil, so it slots right in next to sage without pulling the bed toward the rich, damp conditions sage hates.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cabbage-family crops
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Gardeners plant sage near cabbage to help keep pests away.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Traditional brassica pairing, unverified pest effect. traditional/low.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Sage has long been grown near cabbage, broccoli, and kale in the belief that its strong scent helps deter cabbage pests. Treat this as traditional garden wisdom rather than a proven effect: it is a popular pairing, but no careful study has confirmed the pest benefit, so plant it for the tradition and the convenience, not as guaranteed pest control.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Carrots
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: An old pairing thought to help hide carrots from pests.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Traditional carrot pairing, unverified. traditional/low.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Sage is a traditional carrot neighbor, with growers hoping its aroma helps mask the carrots from carrot fly. This is folk practice with no controlled evidence behind it, so enjoy it as tradition rather than counting on a real pest effect.

bad_seasoned.name: Cucumbers
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional avoid: growers have long held that sage sited next to cucumbers can suppress them, and, more practically, cucumbers want the steady moisture and rich soil that keep sage too wet.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing companion tradition warns against sage near cucumbers. Beyond the folk claim there is a real cultural mismatch: cucumbers need consistent moisture and fertile soil, the opposite of sage's lean, dry ideal, so co-siting forces conditions that rot sage. traditional/low.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Cucumbers
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep cucumbers away from sage; they want very different conditions.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Traditional avoid plus real moisture/soil mismatch. traditional/low.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: There is an old warning against planting sage next to cucumbers, and whatever you make of that, there is a practical reason to keep them apart: cucumbers need steady water and rich soil, while sage needs to stay lean and dry. Growing them together means overwatering the sage, which is the fastest way to rot it.

pests.name: Spittlebugs
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Frothy white spit-like foam on stems in late spring, with a small nymph hidden inside. It looks alarming but rarely harms an established sage plant.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Blobs of white froth like spit on the stems in late spring, with a tiny bug hidden inside. It looks worse than it is.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spittlebug nymphs sheltering in their own foam while sipping sap. Numbers are usually low and damage is mostly cosmetic.
pests.cause_beginner: Young spittlebugs hiding in the foam while they feed. There are usually only a few, and they do little real harm.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock them off with a strong spray of water if you find them unsightly; no treatment is needed for plant health in most cases.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: If the froth bothers you, spray it off with a hose. You usually do not need to do anything else.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Give plants full sun and airflow and do not overwater; vigorous sage shrugs off minor pests.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep sage in full sun with room around it and do not overwater; healthy plants handle small pests.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or bronzing of the leaves and faint webbing, most common on plants in hot, dry, dusty conditions or stressed indoor plants.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves look dusty, speckled, or faded, sometimes with fine webbing, usually in hot dry spells or on indoor plants.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tiny sap-sucking mites that build up in hot, dry, still air, especially on dusty or drought-stressed foliage.
pests.cause_beginner: Very small mites that multiply in hot, dry conditions and feed on the leaves.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse the foliage with a strong spray of water to knock mites down, repeating every few days; insecticidal soap helps in bad cases.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the leaves with water every few days to wash the mites off; insecticidal soap works if there are a lot.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Maintain good airflow, hose off dust in hot spells, and avoid drought stress on containers, which invites mites.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep air moving, rinse dust off in hot weather, and do not let potted sage dry out to the point of stress.

pests.name: Slugs and snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in leaves and slime trails, mainly on young or newly set plants in damp, shady spots.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Chewed, ragged holes in the leaves and shiny slime trails, mostly on young plants in damp shade.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails feeding at night, favored by wet mulch, crowding, and shade around young plants.
pests.cause_beginner: Slugs and snails eating the leaves at night; they like damp, shady, crowded spots.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick at night, remove damp hiding places, and use traps or iron-phosphate bait around vulnerable seedlings.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick them off after dark, clear away damp hiding spots, and use slug traps or an iron-phosphate bait, which carries less risk around pets than the older metaldehyde baits, near young plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant in full sun with good drainage and space plants for airflow; a dry, sunny site is unfriendly to slugs.
pests.prevention_beginner: Give sage a sunny, well-drained, open spot; slugs avoid dry, sunny ground.

pests.name: Leafhoppers
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Occasional small hopping insects on the foliage, more likely on stressed or crowded plants than on healthy sage.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Now and then, tiny hopping bugs on the leaves, usually only on stressed or crowded plants.
pests.cause_seasoned: Sap-feeding insects that occasionally find sage; the plant has few serious pests and rarely needs spraying.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that sometimes turn up. Sage has few pest problems and rarely needs treatment.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse them off with water or use insecticidal soap if numbers climb; improving airflow and removing stress usually resolves it.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, or use insecticidal soap for heavy numbers; more air and less stress usually fixes it.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Full sun, lean soil, and good spacing keep sage unstressed and unattractive to these pests.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep sage in full sun with room around it; healthy plants rarely get these bugs.

diseases.name: Root and stem rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Wilting, yellowing, and dieback that does not recover with watering, often with a darkened, decayed base at the soil line. It is the main disease of sage and is tied to wet soil and poor drainage.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Leaves wilt and yellow and the plant dies back even though the soil is wet, often with a dark, rotted spot where the stems meet the ground. This is the main thing that kills sage, and it comes from staying too wet.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soil-borne water molds and fungi that attack the roots and crown of plants sitting in saturated, poorly drained soil. Wet feet and humid heat, not cold, are the underlying cause.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rot that takes hold when soil stays soggy or the weather is hot and muggy, attacking the roots and base. The real cause is wet soil, not cold.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once the crown is rotting; remove and discard affected plants and fix drainage. Focus on prevention, not rescue.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the base is rotting there is no fix, so pull out and throw away the plant. The answer is preventing it with good drainage, not curing it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, water deeply but infrequently, and never let sage sit wet. On clay, use a mound or raised bed and space plants for airflow.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use well-draining soil in full sun, water deeply but rarely, and never let sage sit in soggy ground. On heavy soil, plant on a mound and give plants room.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A white to gray powdery film on the leaves, most likely in humid weather or on crowded, poorly ventilated plants. It weakens the plant and taints the flavor but is rarely fatal.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A dusty white coating on the leaves, more likely in muggy weather or on crowded plants. It does not usually kill sage but makes it look and taste worse.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungi favored by warm, humid, still air, especially where plants are crowded or shaded. Damp, stagnant conditions raise the risk.
diseases.cause_beginner: Fungi that like warm, damp, still air around crowded plants. Poor airflow makes it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves, thin for airflow, and avoid overhead watering; the spring prune also opens up the canopy.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off the coated leaves, give the plant more air, and water at the soil instead of over the top. The spring trim helps too.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants well, site in full sun, avoid overhead watering, and prune to keep the plant open. Airflow is the main defense.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Leave room between plants, plant in full sun, water at the base, and trim to keep it open. Good air movement is the key.

diseases.name: Verticillium wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sudden wilting and yellowing of branches, sometimes on one side of the plant, that does not recover; a soil-borne wilt that can persist in the ground.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Branches wilt and yellow, often on one side, and do not bounce back. It is a soil disease that can stay in the ground.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soil-borne fungus that plugs the plant's water-conducting tissue. It builds up in soils where susceptible plants are grown repeatedly.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus in the soil that blocks the plant's water pipes. It builds up where the same kinds of plants grow year after year.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure; remove affected plants and avoid replanting sage or other susceptible crops in the same spot. Improve drainage and airflow.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no fix once a plant has it, so remove it and do not replant sage in the same spot. Better drainage and airflow help.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil, rotate the planting site when starting new plants, and avoid ground with a history of wilt.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use well-drained soil, and start new sage in a fresh spot rather than where a wilted plant grew.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Deep and infrequent. Water new plants about weekly through the first season to establish them, then taper sharply; established sage is drought-tolerant and needs water only in extended dry spells, though it produces a bit more with occasional deep watering.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply but not often. A new plant wants about a soak a week the first year; after that, sage needs water only during long dry spells, though a little extra keeps it leafier.
watering.amount_seasoned: Roughly a deep soak once a week while establishing the first season; once mature, water only every couple of weeks in dry weather, letting the soil dry between waterings.
watering.amount_beginner: About a soak a week for a new plant the first year, then much less once it is established.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base and let the soil dry between waterings. Avoid wetting the foliage, which encourages powdery mildew and, with wet soil, root rot.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plant, not over the leaves, and let it dry out before watering again. Wet leaves and soggy soil are what make sage rot.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing leaves, wilting whole shoots, and a plant that fails despite regular watering point to too-wet roots and likely root or stem rot, not drought.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If leaves yellow and shoots wilt even though you are watering, the problem is almost always too much water. Soggy roots rot.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Established sage rarely shows true drought stress; brief midday wilting in extreme heat that recovers overnight is normal and not a reason to increase watering.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Sage almost never gets too little water once established. A little droop on a very hot afternoon that recovers by morning is fine.

schedule_by_stage.rate: about a deep soak once a week
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: The first season is the only time regular watering matters: water a new sage about weekly, a deep soak, to establish it, then taper sharply. Water at the base and keep the foliage dry, since wet leaves encourage powdery mildew and, with wet soil, root rot.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Water a new sage about a soak a week the first year to establish it, then cut back a lot. Water at the base to keep the leaves dry.

schedule_by_stage.rate: a deep soak every couple of weeks in dry weather
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Established sage is drought-tolerant and needs water only in extended dry spells, roughly a deep soak every couple of weeks, letting the soil dry between waterings, though it produces a bit more leaf with occasional deep watering. The most common way to kill it is keeping it too wet, so when in doubt, water less.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Established sage handles dry weather and needs water only during long dry spells, about a soak every couple of weeks, though a little extra keeps it leafier. More sage dies from too much water than too little, so let the soil dry between waterings.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Through dormancy sage wants very little water; keep it on the dry side and do not let the crown sit in wet winter soil.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: In winter sage needs almost no water. Keep it on the dry side and never let it sit in soggy soil.

watering.method_note_seasoned: The most common way to kill sage is keeping it too wet. When in doubt, water less.
watering.method_note_beginner: Remember: more sage dies from too much water than too little.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The first season after planting is the only time regular watering matters; taper off sharply once the plant is established.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Water fairly regularly the first year while it gets established, then back off a lot.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Nursery transplants are already hardened; set them out after the last spring frost. If you start from seed indoors (about 8 to 10 weeks before last frost) or from summer softwood cuttings, harden the young plants gradually before planting out.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you buy a plant, you can set it out after your last spring frost with no fuss. If you grow from seed or cuttings, let the young plants get used to outdoor conditions for a few days first.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Sage is most reliably grown from a nursery transplant or from softwood cuttings, division, or layering, all of which come true to the parent. It can be grown from seed, started indoors roughly 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, but seed is slower and a plant takes about a year to reach good harvesting size, so many growers buy plants or root cuttings instead.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easiest way to grow sage is to buy a small plant or root a cutting from an existing one. You can grow it from seed started indoors about 8 to 10 weeks before your last frost, but seed is slower and takes roughly a year to reach a good size, so most people skip it.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering; sage must never sit in standing water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A free-draining potting mix, not a moisture-holding one.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in coarse sand or perlite so water runs through fast.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A coarse, free-draining potting medium; avoid peat-heavy moisture-retentive mixes.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Add coarse sand or perlite to sharpen drainage.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry faster than the ground, so check the soil, but still let it dry between waterings and never leave the pot in a full saucer.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Container sage needs only a very light feed, if any; do not over-fertilize.

overwintering.approach_beginner: In the coldest zones, grow sage in a pot you can move to a bright, cool, sheltered spot for winter, keeping it on the dry side, then bring it back out in spring.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Where winters are too harsh for reliable in-ground survival, a container lets you overwinter sage under cover in a cool bright space; keep it barely moist and protected from hard freezes, then return it outdoors after frost.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Sage grows well in containers, which is the standard way to keep it going through winter in the coldest zones and to grow the more tender variegated types. Use a wide, free-draining pot and gritty mix, water sparingly, and re-pot into fresh mix as it fills the pot.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Sage does fine in a pot, which is handy if your winters are very cold or you are growing one of the fancy variegated types. Use a wide pot with drainage holes and a gritty mix, water lightly, and tip out any water in the saucer.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers keep the medium too consistently moist for sage and promote root rot; use a conventional free-draining pot instead.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Skip self-watering pots for sage; they keep the soil too wet and the roots rot.

recommended.name: Berggarten
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy in roughly zones 4 to 8; among the hardier culinary sages.
recommended.note: Compact, non-flowering to shy-flowering type with large, rounded silver-green leaves; widely rated one of the best-flavored culinary sages.

recommended.name: Common (Broadleaf)
recommended.note: The standard broad-leaved garden sage, gray-green pebbly leaves, blue-purple flower spikes in early summer; the all-purpose culinary type.

recommended.name: Purpurascens (Purple sage)
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy in roughly zones 5 to 8; slightly less hardy than green types.
recommended.note: Purple-flushed young foliage aging to gray-green; culinary and ornamental, a little less cold-hardy than plain green sage.

recommended.name: Icterina (Golden sage)
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy in roughly zones 6 to 8; less cold-hardy and best with winter protection in cold zones.
recommended.note: Gold-and-green variegated leaves, mild flavor, mainly ornamental but edible; more tender than green sage.

recommended.name: Tricolor
recommended.hardiness_note: Tender, hardy only to about zone 6 to 7; often grown in a container to overwinter.
recommended.note: Showy gray, purple, and cream-white variegated leaves; ornamental and edible but the least cold-hardy and often short-lived.

recommended.name: Extrakta
recommended.note: A high-essential-oil strain grown for strong, consistent flavor and aroma; a good choice where potent seasoning is the goal.

varieties.note_seasoned: The culinary sages here are all forms of Salvia officinalis, differing mainly in leaf color, flavor intensity, and cold-hardiness. Green-leaved types (common Broadleaf, Berggarten, Extrakta) are the hardiest and the workhorse kitchen sages, with Berggarten prized for flavor and a tidy non-flowering habit. Colored-leaf forms (Purpurascens purple sage, Icterina golden sage, Tricolor) are showier and edible but progressively less cold-hardy, and Tricolor especially is tender and often short-lived. Note that pineapple sage is a different species, Salvia elegans, a tender pineapple-scented plant grown for its red flowers, not one of these garden-sage cultivars.
varieties.note_beginner: All the kitchen sages here are types of one plant, Salvia officinalis, that differ in leaf color, strength, and how much cold they take. The plain green kinds (common Broadleaf, Berggarten, Extrakta) are the toughest and the best all-round cooking sages, and Berggarten is a favorite for flavor. The colored-leaf kinds (purple, golden, and tricolor sage) are prettier and still edible, but they are less cold-hardy, and tricolor is the most tender. Heads up: pineapple sage is a different, tender plant (Salvia elegans) grown for its red flowers, not one of these cooking sages.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Fresh-cut sprigs keep a few days in a jar of water on the counter or loosely wrapped. For long keeping, sage is dried rather than stored fresh.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Fresh sprigs last a few days in a glass of water on the counter. For the long term, you dry sage.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Fresh sprigs keep about a week wrapped loosely in a damp paper towel in the refrigerator crisper.
storage.fridge_beginner: Fresh sage keeps about a week in the fridge, wrapped in a slightly damp paper towel.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Leaves freeze well, whole or chopped in oil in ice-cube trays, keeping much of their flavor for several months.
storage.freezer_beginner: You can freeze sage leaves, whole or chopped in a little oil in an ice-cube tray, to use later.
storage.notes_seasoned: To dry sage, cut stems in the morning after the dew dries, tie them in small loose bunches, and hang them upside down in a warm, dark, airy place, or dry the leaves on screens. Once crisp, strip the leaves and store them whole in a sealed, opaque container away from light and heat, where they keep good flavor for up to a year.
storage.notes_beginner: Dry sage by cutting stems in the morning, tying them in small bunches, and hanging them upside down somewhere warm, dark, and airy. When the leaves are crisp, strip them off and keep them whole in a sealed jar out of the light, where they hold their flavor for up to a year.

rotation.note_seasoned: N/A. Sage is a perennial that stays in place for several years, so annual crop rotation does not apply. When starting new plants, choose a fresh, well-drained site rather than replanting where an old sage or a wilt-prone crop grew, to avoid carrying over soil-borne rot or verticillium wilt.
rotation.note_beginner: N/A. Sage is not rotated like a vegetable because it stays put for years. When you replace an old plant, pick a fresh, well-draining spot rather than the exact place the old one grew.

growth_stages.name: Plant out
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Set nursery plants out after the last spring frost in a sunny, well-drained spot, spacing them 18 to 24 inches apart. On heavy ground, plant on a mound or raised bed rather than digging sand into clay.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: After your last spring frost, plant the sage in a sunny, well-draining spot, about 18 to 24 inches apart so each plant has room and airflow.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A compact young plant with gray-green foliage and firm roots filling the nursery pot, ready to set out once frost has passed.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A small bushy plant with soft gray-green leaves and roots that hold the potting soil together when you slide it out.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Loosen the rootball, set the crown level with the soil surface, and water in once. Do not amend with rich compost or fertilizer; sage wants lean ground.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Gently loosen the roots, plant so the top of the rootball is level with the soil, water once, and skip the fertilizer.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Planted: type or cultivar, number set out, and the date.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Wrote down which sage you planted and when.

growth_stages.name: Establishment (year one)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first season after planting. Sage spends year one building roots, so harvest lightly and let the plant fill out; it reaches good size by about the second year.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first growing season. Your sage is busy growing roots, so go easy on harvesting; it fills out by around the second year.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady new gray-green growth and a plant shaping up bushy rather than stretching. A few flower spikes may appear.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: New gray-green leaves filling in, and maybe a few flower spikes. You want it growing bushy, not tall and leggy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water regularly until settled, then taper toward deep, infrequent watering. Harvest sparingly and pinch to shape. Hold off on fertilizer.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Water fairly often until it takes hold, then water deeply but less often. Harvest just a little and pinch it to stay bushy. Do not feed it.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Establishment: planting-out date, watering taper, and any light shaping.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when you planted it and that you are watering less as it settles.

growth_stages.name: Spring regrowth and harvest
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Each spring the plant breaks fresh green growth and enters its best leaf-harvest window. This is when to make the annual spring prune and to cut sprigs freely.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Every spring, new green growth appears and the best leaf-picking season begins. This is when you do the yearly trim and start cutting sprigs.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New soft green shoots emerging along the stems and crown, the signal the plant came through winter and the flavor is at its peak before flowering.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Soft green shoots coming out in spring. That is your cue the plant survived winter and the leaves taste their best now.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Prune hard as growth breaks, cutting leggy stems back but never into bare old wood. Then harvest sprigs freely and begin deep, infrequent watering.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Trim it back as new growth starts, cutting the leggy stems but not into the hard old wood. Then snip sprigs whenever you cook and water deeply but not often.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Spring: date green growth appeared, the spring prune, and first harvests.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Wrote down when spring growth started and when you trimmed and harvested.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Early summer, when short spikes of blue-purple flowers appear. Leaf flavor is strongest just before bloom, so many cooks pinch the spikes to keep the foliage prime; the flowers feed bees if left.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Early summer, when sage puts up blue-purple flower spikes. The leaves taste best just before it flowers, so many people snip the flowers off; if you leave them, the bees will enjoy them.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Blue-purple flower spikes rising above the foliage. Leaf oils dip slightly during heavy bloom, so harvest for drying just beforehand.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Blue-purple flowers on spikes above the leaves. The leaves are a touch milder while it flowers, so cut any for drying just before.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Decide whether to enjoy the flowers or pinch them for leaf quality. Keep watering deep and infrequent and do not feed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Choose to enjoy the flowers or pinch them off for better leaves. Keep watering deeply but rarely, and do not fertilize.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Bloom: first-open date and whether you kept or pinched the flowers.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when it bloomed and whether you left or removed the flowers.

growth_stages.name: Post-bloom tidy
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: After flowering fades, remove the spent flower spikes and lightly shape the plant. This is a light tidy, not the main structural cut; the hard renewal prune belongs in spring.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Once the flowers fade, snip off the old flower stems and lightly shape the plant. This is just a tidy-up; the big trim happens in spring.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Browning, spent flower spikes and a plant finished with its main bloom. Below the green you will see bare woody stems; these are the no-cut zone.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Faded, brown flower stems and a plant done blooming. Notice the hard woody stems below the green and do not cut into those.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Snip off spent flower stems and tidy stray growth, staying in green wood only. Save any hard cutting for spring, when the plant renews.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut off the old flower stems and tidy it up, staying in the green. Leave any big cutting for spring.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Post-bloom: date you removed spent flowers and any light shaping.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Wrote down when you cleaned up the spent flowers.

growth_stages.name: Dormancy (cold zones)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: In zones with freezing winters, sage slows or stops and holds much of its gray foliage as a semi-evergreen. It needs almost no water, and wet soil, not cold alone, is what usually kills it over winter.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Where winters freeze, sage mostly stops growing and keeps a lot of its gray leaves. It barely needs water, and soggy soil, not the cold, is what usually kills it.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A plant that has stopped growing for the season. Hardy green types hold their foliage; tender variegated types decline in cold and need protection or to come indoors.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A plant that has stopped growing. The tough green kinds keep their leaves; the tender variegated kinds fade in the cold and need shelter.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Stop watering and feeding, and leave hard pruning for spring. Protect tender types or move container plants under cover. In the coldest zones, mulch or a sheltered spot helps.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Stop watering and feeding, and save the big trim for spring. Shelter the tender kinds or bring pots somewhere protected. In very cold areas, mulch or a sheltered spot helps.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Dormancy: date growth stopped and any winter protection applied.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when it went dormant and any winter cover you added.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your plant-out window is open. Set nursery plants in full sun in well-drained soil after the last frost, spacing them 18 to 24 inches apart. Skip the rich compost and fertilizer.
notifications.body_beginner: It is time to plant your sage. Put it in a sunny, well-draining spot now that frost has passed, 18 to 24 inches apart, and do not add fertilizer.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to prune and start harvesting sage
notifications.title_beginner: Time to trim and pick your sage
notifications.body_seasoned: New spring growth is breaking. Prune leggy stems back into green wood (never into the bare old wood), then harvest sprigs freely; flavor peaks now, before flowering.
notifications.body_beginner: Fresh spring growth is showing. Trim the leggy stems back to green (not into the hard wood), then start snipping sprigs, since the flavor is best now before it flowers.

notifications.title_beginner: Get your sage ready for winter
notifications.body_seasoned: Cold is coming. Stop watering and feeding, leave hard pruning for spring, and protect tender variegated types or move container plants under cover. Wet winter soil, not cold, is the usual killer.
notifications.body_beginner: Winter is coming. Stop watering and feeding, save the big trim for spring, and shelter the tender variegated kinds or bring pots somewhere protected. Soggy soil, not the cold, is what usually kills sage.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Late frost on tender new growth
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Late frost on the new growth
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A late spring frost is forecast while sage is pushing tender new growth. Hold off on the hard spring prune until frost has fully passed, and protect newly set-out plants overnight.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A late spring frost is coming while your sage has soft new growth. Wait to do the big trim until frost is fully over, and cover any just-planted sage overnight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Humid heat raises rot and mildew risk
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot, humid weather raises rot and mildew risk
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A spell of humid heat is forecast, which raises the risk of root and stem rot, powdery mildew, and gray mold in muggy regions. Do not add water on sage's account, make sure it is not sitting wet, and keep airflow open around the plant.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot, sticky weather is coming, which can bring rot and powdery mildew. Do not give sage extra water, make sure it is not sitting in wet soil, and keep the area around it open and airy.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Wet winter soil is the real risk
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Soggy winter soil is the real risk
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Prolonged wet soil is forecast heading into or during winter dormancy. Wet winter ground, not cold, is what usually kills sage, so make sure it is not sitting in water and consider moving containers under cover.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A long wet spell is coming around winter. Soggy soil, not the cold, is what usually kills sage, so make sure it is not standing in water, and move pots somewhere protected if you can.

transplant.text_seasoned: Plant sage lean and dry, not rich. Skip the compost-and-fertilizer routine other plants want, give it your sunniest, best-draining spot, and on clay build a mound or raised bed. Wet, rich soil is what kills sage.
transplant.text_beginner: Sage does best in poor, dry soil, so do not add fertilizer or rich compost. Give it your sunniest spot, and if your soil is heavy clay, plant it on a little mound so water drains away.

transplant.text_seasoned: Space plants 18 to 24 inches apart. Good airflow between plants is one of the simplest ways to head off the powdery mildew and rot sage is prone to in damp conditions.
transplant.text_beginner: Leave about 18 to 24 inches between plants. That space lets air move around each one, which helps prevent the mildew and rot sage can get when it stays damp.

establishment.text_seasoned: Year one is about roots, not harvest. Water regularly until settled, then taper to deep and infrequent. Harvest lightly so the plant can bulk up; it reaches good size by about the second year.
establishment.text_beginner: The first year is about growing roots. Water fairly often until it takes hold, then water deeply but less often. Harvest just a little so the plant can fill out; it gets to a good size by around the second year.

establishment.text_seasoned: Resist the urge to feed. Sage has low fertility needs, and over-feeding gives soft growth with weaker flavor. The same goes for water: more is not better.
establishment.text_beginner: Try not to feed it. Sage needs very little, and too much fertilizer gives floppy growth and weaker-tasting leaves. The same is true for water, where more is not better.

vegetative.text_seasoned: Prune hard in spring as new growth breaks. Cut leggy stems back but never into the bare old wood, which resprouts poorly. This yearly cut keeps sage compact and slows the woody decline, though plants still need replacing every few years.
vegetative.text_beginner: Trim sage back in spring when new growth starts. Cut the leggy stems but not down into the hard old wood, which does not grow back well. This yearly trim keeps it bushy and slows it going woody, but you will still replace plants every few years.

vegetative.text_seasoned: Spring into early summer is the best harvest window. Cut sprigs freely from new growth, taking no more than about half the plant, and harvest in mid-morning after the dew dries for the strongest flavor.
vegetative.text_beginner: Spring and early summer is the best time to pick. Snip sprigs from the new growth, never more than about half the plant, and cut in mid-morning once the dew has dried for the best flavor.

bloom.text_seasoned: Leaf flavor peaks just before bloom. If cooking is your goal, pinch the flower spikes to keep the foliage prime; if you value pollinators, leave them, since bees and butterflies work the blue-purple flowers.
bloom.text_beginner: The leaves taste best just before it flowers. If you grow sage to cook with, snip the flower spikes off to keep the leaves good; if you like pollinators, leave them for the bees and butterflies.

bloom.text_seasoned: Cut sage for drying just before it flowers, then hang small bunches upside down somewhere warm, dark, and airy. Strip the crisp leaves whole into a sealed jar out of the light.
bloom.text_beginner: Cut sage for drying right before it flowers, then hang small bunches upside down somewhere warm and airy. When crisp, strip the leaves into a sealed jar kept out of the light.

cut_back.text_seasoned: After bloom, remove spent flower stems and lightly tidy the plant, staying in green wood. Save the hard renewal prune for spring; cutting deep into old wood late in the season leaves sage weak going into winter.
cut_back.text_beginner: After it flowers, snip off the old flower stems and tidy it up, staying in the green. Leave the big trim for spring; cutting hard into the woody parts late in the year leaves sage weak for winter.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Over winter, do almost nothing: stop watering and feeding, and leave hard pruning for spring. A dormant plant in wet soil rots, so the worst thing you can do is keep it wet.
dormancy.text_beginner: In winter, do almost nothing. Stop watering and feeding, and save the big trim for spring. A resting plant in wet soil rots, so do not keep it wet.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Protect the tender types. Variegated sages like Tricolor and golden Icterina are less cold-hardy and are best in containers brought under cover for winter, while green types overwinter outdoors through about zone 4 with sharp drainage and shelter.
dormancy.text_beginner: Shelter the tender kinds. Variegated sages like tricolor and golden sage are less cold-hardy, so grow them in pots you can bring somewhere protected for winter. The plain green kinds can stay outside in cold zones if they have good drainage and a sheltered spot.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature plant supplies far more leaves than most kitchens use: cut sprigs through the season for fresh use plus bundles to dry. A single healthy plant typically covers a household's culinary sage, with production best from about the second year until the plant turns woody.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One healthy sage plant gives you more leaves than you will probably use, fresh through the season and extra to dry. It produces best from about the second year until it gets woody.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Harvest lightly the first year while the plant establishes; heavier cutting can wait until it has filled out, around the second season.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Go easy on harvesting the first year while the plant settles in. Cut more once it has filled out, around year two.
factors_seasoned: Plant age and size (best production from about year two until it turns woody)
Full sun and lean, well-drained soil for strong flavor
Regular light harvest and an annual spring prune to keep growth young and flavorful
Cultivar (green broadleaf and Berggarten types are the workhorse culinary sages)

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves turning yellow or the plant dying back
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: With sage, yellowing and dieback almost always mean too wet, not too dry. Overwatering, poor drainage, or humid heat lead to root and stem rot. The plant is drowning, not thirsty.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: For sage, yellow leaves and dieback usually mean too much water, not too little. Overwatering, soggy soil, or muggy heat cause root and stem rot. The plant is drowning, not thirsty.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cut back on watering and fix drainage. Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, water deeply but infrequently, and on clay use a mound or raised bed. Never let sage sit wet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water much less and improve drainage. Use poor, well-draining soil in full sun, water deeply but only now and then, and on heavy soil plant on a mound. Never let it sit in soggy ground.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Sage naturally turns woody and sprawls with age, and it happens faster without the yearly spring prune. Old wood does not resprout well, so a badly overgrown plant is hard to renew.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Sage gets woody and floppy as it ages, and faster if it is not trimmed each spring. The hard old wood does not grow back well, so a very overgrown plant is hard to fix.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Prune each spring as growth breaks, cutting leggy stems back into green wood but never into bare old wood. Even so, sage is short-lived, so plan to replace plants every few years from cuttings or new stock.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Trim every spring when new growth starts, cutting the leggy stems back to green but not into the hard wood. Sage is short-lived anyway, so plan to replace it every few years with a cutting or a new plant.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Weak flavor or sparse, floppy growth
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Weak taste or thin, floppy growth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Bland leaves and soft, leggy growth usually mean too much shade, too much water, or too much feeding. Sage develops its strong flavor in full sun and lean, dry soil, and over-rich conditions dilute it.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Weak-tasting leaves and floppy growth usually mean too little sun or too much water or fertilizer. Sage gets its strong flavor from full sun and poor, dry soil, and pampering waters it down.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Move it to full sun, stop feeding, and water sparingly. Harvest regularly and prune in spring to keep young, flavorful growth coming.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Give it full sun, stop feeding it, and water less. Pick it often and trim in spring to keep fresh, tasty growth coming.

Plant-out runs from the warmest zone's last spring frost (about mid-March in zone 7) to the coldest zone's (late spring in zone 3); sage is set out as a nursery transplant after the last spring frost. plantings.synthesis_note_beginner: These cover the whole northern tier. Set sage out after your last spring frost, anywhere from mid-March in the mildest spots to late spring in the coldest. It flowers in early summer, a little sooner in the warmer zones and later in the coldest ones.

3.grown_as_note_seasoned: Annual or container. Zone 3 is below common sage's hardy range, so it is grown as a single-season plant or as a container plant brought in for winter. With a short frost-free season, set nursery transplants out promptly after the last spring frost to get a full season of leaves and a first-summer bloom before frost ends the year.
3.grown_as_note_beginner: Sage will not survive a zone 3 winter outdoors, so grow it for the season or in a pot you bring inside. Summers are short here, so plant it as soon as your last spring frost has passed to get a season of leaves.
3.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Too cold to overwinter reliably in the ground here, so grow sage as an annual or in a container moved under cover for winter. Set plants out only after the last spring frost; the outdoor season ends at the first fall frost.
3.synthesis_note_seasoned: grown_as=annual: zone 3 does not support reliable in-ground overwintering (cold in the north, heat-and-humidity in the subtropics), so sage is carried as a replanted annual. plant_out and bloom drive the plant / growing / bloom / season_over calendar; no dormant or prune token. plant_out 'May - Jun'; bloom 'Jul - Aug'. Cold-zone first-season windows are frost-resolved from the general early-summer bloom phenology, not a zone-specific sage chart. Flagged blocks_launch:false.

4.grown_as_note_seasoned: Perennial at the cold edge. Zone 4 is the cold limit of common sage (hardy to about zone 4), so it overwinters in the ground only with sharp drainage and winter protection, and is often short-lived. Many gardeners here treat it as a bring-in container plant or replace it each year to be safe.
4.grown_as_note_beginner: Sage can just survive a zone 4 winter, but only with excellent drainage and some protection, and it is often short-lived. Many people grow it in a pot they can shelter, or simply replace it each year to be safe.
4.frost_risk_note_seasoned: At the cold edge of sage's range. It overwinters in the ground only with sharp drainage and winter protection and is often short-lived; a bring-in container plant is the safer bet. Set plants out after the last spring frost.
4.synthesis_note_seasoned: grown_as=perennial (cold edge): common sage is hardy to about zone 4, so zone 4 is modeled as an in-ground perennial that survives only with sharp drainage and winter protection and is often short-lived. Dormancy is frost-bracketed from this zone's frost dates; bloom is the early-summer window; the single prune token is the post-bloom tidy, with the main renewal prune covered as a spring task in the care prose. plant_out 'Apr - May'; bloom 'Jun - Jul'. Cold-zone first-season windows are frost-resolved from the general early-summer bloom phenology, not a zone-specific sage chart. Flagged blocks_launch:false.

5.grown_as_note_seasoned: Perennial. In zone 5, common green sage overwinters in the ground as a woody subshrub, leafing out in spring, blooming in early summer, and renewed by a spring prune. Give it sharp drainage and it persists several years before turning woody; tender variegated types still need winter protection.
5.grown_as_note_beginner: Sage comes back year after year in zone 5. It grows in the ground, flowers in early summer, and gets a trim each spring. Give it good drainage and it lasts several years before getting woody. The fancy variegated kinds still need winter protection.
5.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Hardy enough to overwinter in the ground with sharp drainage; give tender variegated types winter protection. Set new plants out after the last spring frost, and do the hard renewal prune in spring, not fall.

description_seasoned: Sage (Salvia officinalis), also called common, garden, or culinary sage, is a woody Mediterranean perennial subshrub in the mint family, grown for its aromatic, pebbly-textured, gray-green leaves used fresh or dried in cooking. This is the culinary kitchen sage, not the ornamental bedding salvias (such as scarlet or mealycup sage) sold as annual flowers. It carries short spikes of blue-purple flowers in early summer that bees and butterflies love, but the leaves are the crop, and many cooks pinch the flower spikes to keep the foliage flavorful. Sage thrives on lean treatment: full sun, poor to average well-drained soil, and little water or feeding. It is one of the hardier culinary herbs, reliably perennial in much of the country, but it is short-lived and turns woody and sprawling with age, so plan to replace plants every few years and prune each spring to slow the decline. Overwatering and humid heat, not cold, are what usually kill it, through root and stem rot.
description_beginner: Sage is a small woody herb with soft gray-green leaves that you use in cooking, fresh or dried. It comes from the dry Mediterranean, so it wants full sun, poor well-drained soil, and not much water. This is kitchen sage (Salvia officinalis), not the colorful flower salvias sold as annuals. It makes pretty blue-purple flower spikes in early summer that bees love, but you grow it for the leaves, so many people snip the flowers off. Sage is one of the tougher herbs and comes back year after year in much of the country, but plants get woody and leggy after a few years, so trim it each spring and plan to replace it every few years. Too much water or hot, muggy weather, not cold, is what usually rots and kills it.
harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest sage leaves and sprigs as needed once the plant is growing well. Harvest lightly the first year while the plant establishes, then cut more freely. Flavor is strongest in new growth from spring into early summer and just before flowering, so that is the best window for drying. Cut sprigs about 6 to 8 inches from the tips, taking no more than about half the plant at once, and harvest in mid-morning after the dew dries, when leaf oils are highest. On evergreen plants in mild climates you can pick a few leaves any time of year.
harvest_ready_beginner: Snip sage leaves and sprigs whenever you cook once the plant is growing well. Go easy the first year, then cut more freely. The flavor is best on fresh spring and early-summer growth and just before it flowers, which is also the best time to cut some for drying. Take sprigs about 6 to 8 inches from the top, never more than about half the plant at once, and cut in mid-morning after the dew dries for the strongest flavor. In mild climates sage stays leafy, so you can pick a few leaves any time.
hardiness_notes_seasoned: Common sage (Salvia officinalis) is hardy in roughly USDA zones 4 to 8, one of the hardier culinary herbs, and reliably perennial through much of the country. It is short-lived even so, turning woody and sprawling within a few years, so plan to replace plants every three to five years and prune each spring to slow the decline. Green-leaved types are the hardiest; variegated forms (Tricolor, golden Icterina, purple Purpurascens) are progressively more tender. In the coldest zones (zone 3 and marginal zone 4) and in humid subtropical heat, sage is short-lived or best grown as an annual or a bring-in container plant.
hardiness_notes_beginner: Sage is one of the tougher herbs and comes back year after year in most of the country (about zones 4 to 8). Even so, plants get woody and leggy within a few years, so trim them each spring and plan to replace them every few years. The plain green kinds are the hardiest; the colorful variegated types are less cold-hardy. In the very coldest areas and in hot, muggy climates, sage is short-lived, so many people grow it for a season or in a pot they can bring inside for winter.
year_one_notes_seasoned: In the first year, focus on establishment: water regularly until the plant is settled, then taper off, and harvest lightly so the plant can build a bushy framework. Pinch to shape rather than cutting hard. Sage reaches good harvesting size by about the second year and produces best from then until it turns woody.
year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about getting the plant established. Water it fairly regularly until it takes hold, then cut back on water, and only harvest a little so it can fill out. Sage reaches a good size by about the second year, and that is when it really starts producing.
soil_prep_seasoned: Choose the sunniest, best-draining spot you have. Sage wants lean, well-drained soil, so work in only a little coarse compost and skip heavy fertility. On heavy clay, improve drainage with a raised bed or mound rather than digging sand into the clay, which can make drainage worse. The goal is dry feet, not rich ground.
soil_prep_beginner: Pick the sunniest spot with the best drainage. Mix a little coarse compost into the top of the soil, but keep it lean. If your ground is heavy clay, plant sage in a raised bed or mound instead, because that drains better. The goal is dry, well-drained soil, not rich soil.
bloom_time_beginner: Sage makes blue-purple flower spikes in early summer, sooner in warm areas and later in cold ones. Since you grow it for the leaves, flowering is up to you: the leaves taste best just before it blooms, so many people snip the flowers off, while others leave them for the bees. When yours blooms depends on where you live.
bloom_time_seasoned: Sage carries short spikes of blue-purple flowers in early summer, a little earlier in warm regions and later in cold ones. It is grown for its leaves, so flowering is optional; leaf flavor peaks just before bloom, and many cooks pinch the spikes, while others leave them for bees and butterflies. Exact timing shifts with your region and is set per zone.

dormancy_window.note_seasoned: In zones with freezing winters, sage slows and holds much of its gray foliage as a semi-evergreen. Stop watering and feeding, leave hard pruning for spring, and protect tender variegated types or move container plants under cover. A dormant plant needs almost no water, and it is wet soil, not the cold itself, that usually rots or kills it over winter.
dormancy_window.note_beginner: Where winters freeze, sage mostly stops growing but keeps a lot of its gray leaves. Stop watering and feeding it, save any big trim for spring, and in cold areas shelter the tender variegated kinds or bring pots somewhere protected. A resting plant barely needs water, and it is usually soggy soil, not the cold, that kills sage over winter.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Sage is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer partner. It is grown for its leaves, not fruit or seed, so no cross-pollination planning is required. Its blue-purple flowers are highly attractive to bees and butterflies if left to bloom.
pollination.notes_beginner: You only need one sage plant, and it does not need a partner plant. You grow it for the leaves, so pollination does not matter for your harvest. Bees and butterflies love the flowers if you let it bloom, which is a nice bonus.

pruning_window.note_seasoned: Prune sage hard in spring as new growth breaks, cutting leggy stems back but never into the bare old wood, which resprouts poorly. Follow with light trims and sprig harvests through the season, and remove spent flower stems after bloom. This yearly renewal keeps the plant compact and flavorful and slows the woody decline, but sage is short-lived, so plan to replace plants every few years.
pruning_window.note_beginner: Trim sage back each spring when new growth appears, cutting the leggy stems but not down into the hard woody base, which will not grow back well. Keep it tidy with light trims and by snipping sprigs through the season, and cut off the old flower stems after it blooms. This keeps sage bushy and tasty, but plants still get woody after a few years and are worth replacing.
